*Figure 4: The a. Kruskal and b. Penrose diagrams for the AdS2 “black hole.” The shaded wedge denotes the region causally accessible to the right accelerating quark.*

To implement the above procedure in detail,99 9 See [47] for the four-point scattering analysis in Einstein gravity and [53, 32] for its adaptation to the worldsheet. we first write the correlator as an overlap between two states:

$$ \displaystyle\langle W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}U_{1}\rangle \displaystyle=\langle\text{out}|\text{in}\rangle. $$

Here, we have used a cyclic permutation to move $U(\theta_{1})$ to the rightmost position in the correlator in (5.1) and we have defined the states

$$ \displaystyle|\rm in\rangle \displaystyle=W_{6}V_{4}U_{1}|0\rangle, \displaystyle|\rm out\rangle \displaystyle=V_{3}^{\dagger}U_{2}^{\dagger}W_{5}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. $$

These are naturally interpreted as “in” and “out” states for three particles propagating in AdS2, which we can understand heuristically as follows (see [47]). In setting up the “in” state, we start with the vacuum $|0\rangle$ at $t=0$ , evolve forward to time $T_{1}>0$ and act with the operator $U$ to create a particle on the boundary, evolve to time $T_{2}>0$ and create a second particle on the boundary, and, finally, evolve all the way back to time $T_{3}<0$ and act with $W$ to create a third particle on the boundary. We assume that the particles move along lightlike trajectories as we evolve forward and backward in time and that they propagate freely unless their trajectories cross. Given the order in which we act with $U$ , $V$ and $W$ on the vacuum state, the trajectories of the three particles do not cross while setting up the state, so the end result of this procedure is to produce three separated particles in the far past, two of which are right-moving particles (carrying positive lightcone momentum $p^{u}$ ) in the bottom left of the Penrose diagram and one of which is a left-moving particle (carrying positive lightcone momentum $p^{v}$ ) in the bottom right of the Penrose diagram.1010 10 One might ask whether it is sensible to define asymptotic in and out states on the two dimensional worldsheet that involve two or more massless particles moving in the same direction, given that the particles do not become well-separated in either the infinite past or the infinite future and therefore ostensibly interact “forever.” This is a reasonable objection, but for the purpose of performing a check of the analytically continued six-point function by comparing it with a scattering amplitude on the worldsheet, it appears to be valid to ignore the interactions between the parallel-moving $U$ and $V$ particles. Intuitively, this seems to be related to the fact that $U$ and $V$ are in relative time order in (5.6). Nonetheless, it would be good to have a better understanding of the subtleties associated with massless scattering in two dimensions. A related discussion can be found in section 2 of [39]. An analogous interpretation can be given to the out state. The in and out states are depicted in Figure 5.

*Figure 5: In and out scattering states for the six-point OTOC.*

Next, we write the in and out states in terms of in and out Kruskal momentum eigenstates:

$$ \displaystyle|\rm in\rangle \displaystyle=\int dp_{1}^{v}dp_{4}^{v}dp_{6}^{u}\Phi_{\Delta_{U}}(p_{1}^{v},t_{1})\Phi_{\Delta_{V}}(p_{4}^{v},t_{4})\Psi_{\Delta_{W}}(p_{6}^{u},t_{6})|p_{1}^{v},p_{4}^{v},p_{6}^{u}\rangle_{\rm in}, \displaystyle\ |\rm out\rangle \displaystyle=\int dp_{2}^{v}dp_{3}^{v}dp_{5}^{u}\Phi_{\Delta_{U}}(p_{2}^{v},t_{2}^{*})\Phi_{\Delta_{V}}(p_{3}^{v},t_{3}^{*})\Psi_{\Delta_{W}}(p_{5}^{u},t_{5}^{*})|p_{2}^{v},p_{3}^{v},p_{5}^{u}\rangle_{\rm out}. $$

Here, $\Phi_{\Delta}(p^{v},t)$ is the momentum-space wavefunction for a right-moving particle with lightcone momentum $p^{v}$ that is created by a local operator of conformal dimension $\Delta$ acting at lorentzian time $t$ on the right AdS2 boundary; likewise $\Psi_{\Delta}(p^{u},t)$ is the wavefunction for a left-moving particle with lightcone momentum $p^{u}$ . We use $t=-i\theta$ to denote the Lorentzian time, and in (5.9) we used $O(t)^{\dagger}=O(t^{*})$ if $O$ is Hermitian. Finally, we take the momentum eigenstates to be normalized as

$$ \displaystyle{{}_{\rm in}\langle p|q\rangle_{\rm in}}={{}_{\rm out}\langle p|q\rangle_{\rm out}}=p\delta(p-q). $$

Taking the inner product of (5.8) and (5.9), the OTOC in (5.2) can be expressed as the following amplitude:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\rm out|in\rangle \displaystyle=\int\prod_{i}dp_{i}\Phi_{\Delta_{U}}(p_{2}^{v},t_{2}^{*})^{*}\Phi_{\Delta_{V}}(p_{3}^{v},t_{3}^{*})^{*}\Psi_{\Delta_{W}}(p_{5}^{u},t_{5}^{*})^{*}\text{ }_{\rm out}\langle p_{2}^{v},p_{3}^{v},p_{5}^{u}|p_{1}^{v},p_{4}^{v},p_{6}^{u}\rangle_{\rm in} \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\times\Phi_{\Delta_{U}}(p_{1}^{v},t_{1})\Phi_{\Delta_{V}}(p_{4}^{v},t_{4})\Psi_{\Delta_{W}}(p_{6}^{u},t_{6}) $$

To evaluate this expression, we need to know the momentum-space S-matrix and the wavefunctions. The wavefunctions are simply the Fourier transforms of the boundary-to-bulk propagator with respect to $u$ on the $v=0$ horizon and with respect to $v$ on the $u=0$ horizon, respectively. Explicitly, they are [53, 54, 32]

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\Delta}(p^{u},t_{i}) \displaystyle=\theta(p^{u})\frac{(2ip^{u}v_{i})^{\Delta}}{\sqrt{\Gamma(2\Delta)}p^{u}}e^{2ip^{u}v_{i}}, \displaystyle\Phi_{\Delta}(p^{v},t_{i}) \displaystyle=\theta(p^{v})\frac{(2ip^{v}u_{i})^{\Delta}}{\sqrt{\Gamma(2\Delta)}p^{v}}e^{2ip^{v}u_{i}}. $$

where $(u_{i},v_{i})=(-e^{-t_{i}},e^{t_{i}})$ for the points on the boundary.

Furthermore, the momentum space S-matrix takes a very simple form, assuming that the two high energy scattering events are governed by the flat-space S-matrix derived in [39]. In that work, the $2$ -to- $2$ S-matrix for two particles with momenta $p^{u}$ and $p^{v}$ was found to be a phase with exponent proportional to the center-of-mass energy $s=4p^{u}p^{v}$ :

$$ \displaystyle|p^{u},p^{v}\rangle_{\rm out} \displaystyle=e^{-i\ell_{s}^{2}p^{u}p^{v}}|p^{u},p^{v}\rangle_{\rm in}. $$

In our case, we have a $3\to 3$ scattering event, which we assume factorizes into two $2$ -to- $2$ scattering events:

$$ \displaystyle|p_{2}^{v},p_{3}^{v},p_{5}^{u}\rangle_{\rm out}=e^{-i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{2}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}e^{-i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{3}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}|p_{2}^{v},p_{3}^{v},p_{5}^{u}\rangle_{\rm in}. $$

It follows that

$$ {}_{\rm out}\langle p_{2}^{v},p_{3}^{v},p_{5}^{u}|p_{1}^{v},p_{4}^{v},p_{6}^{u}\rangle_{\rm in} \displaystyle=e^{i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{1}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}e^{i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{3}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}p_{1}^{v}p_{3}^{v}p_{5}^{u}\delta(p_{1}^{v}-p_{2}^{v})\delta(p_{3}^{v}-p_{4}^{v})\delta(p_{5}^{u}-p_{6}^{u}). $$

Substituting (5.12) and (5.15) into (5.11), we find the scattering representation of the OTOC to be

$$ \displaystyle\langle\rm out|in\rangle \displaystyle=(4u_{1}u_{2})^{\Delta_{U}}(4u_{3}u_{4})^{\Delta_{V}}(4v_{5}v_{6})^{\Delta_{W}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dp_{1}^{v}dp_{3}^{v}dp_{5}^{u}\biggr[\frac{(p_{1}^{v})^{2\Delta_{U}-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{U})}\frac{(p_{3}^{v})^{2\Delta_{V}-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{V})}\frac{(p_{5}^{u})^{2\Delta_{W}-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{W})} \displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\times e^{2ip_{1}^{v}(u_{1}-u_{2})}e^{2ip_{3}^{v}(u_{4}-u_{3})}e^{2ip_{5}^{u}(v_{6}-v_{5})}e^{i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{1}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}e^{i\ell_{s}^{2}p_{3}^{v}p_{5}^{u}}\biggr]. $$

Changing the momentum integration variables to $p=-2ip_{1}^{v}(u_{1}-u_{2})$ , $q=-2ip_{3}^{v}(u_{4}-u_{3})$ , $\phi=-2ip_{5}^{u}(v_{6}-v_{5})$ , and also normalizing the six-point function by the two-point functions,

$$ \displaystyle\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{1}{[2\sin\left(\frac{it_{12}}{2}\right)]^{2\Delta_{U}}}=\left[-\frac{u_{1}u_{2}}{(u_{1}-u_{2})^{2}}\right]^{\Delta_{U}}, $$

with analogous expressions for $\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle$ and $\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle$ , we arrive at the following expression for the normalized OTOC:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle} \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}dpdqd\phi\frac{p^{2\Delta_{U}-1}q^{2\Delta_{V}-1}\phi^{2\Delta_{W}-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{U})\Gamma(2\Delta_{V})\Gamma(2\Delta_{W})}e^{-p-q-\phi-\kappa_{1}p\phi-\kappa_{2}q\phi}. $$

Here, we have introduced

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{-i\ell_{s}^{2}}{4(u_{1}-u_{2})(v_{5}-v_{6})}=-\frac{i\ell_{s}^{2}e^{(t_{1}+t_{2}-t_{5}-t_{6})/2}}{16\sinh\left(\frac{t_{12}}{2}\right)\sinh\left(\frac{t_{56}}{2}\right)}, \displaystyle\kappa_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{i\ell_{s}^{2}}{4(u_{3}-u_{4})(v_{5}-v_{6})}=\frac{i\ell_{s}^{2}e^{(t_{3}+t_{4}-t_{5}-t_{6})/2}}{16\sinh\left(\frac{t_{34}}{2}\right)\sinh\left(\frac{t_{56}}{2}\right)}. $$

For the configuration in (5.2) with the $\delta_{i}$ given in (5.3) and with $t_{i}=-i\theta_{i}$ , $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ become:

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{8\sqrt{3}T_{s}}, \displaystyle\kappa_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{e^{T_{23}}}{8\sqrt{3}T_{s}}. $$

We can evaluate the integrals over $p$ and $q$ in (5.18) to get:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{W})}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\phi\phi^{2\Delta_{W}-1}(1+\kappa_{1}\phi)^{-2\Delta_{U}}(1+\kappa_{2}\phi)^{-2\Delta_{V}}e^{-\phi}. $$

To get the behavior of the OTOC at strong-coupling, we can expand in $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ and evaluate the integrals order by order.1111 11 Another regime in which we can evaluate (5.23) analytically is when $\Delta_{U},\Delta_{V}\gg 1$ . Then we can use a saddle point approximation to derive: $\displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle}$ $\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{(1+2\kappa_{1}\Delta_{U}+2\kappa_{2}\Delta_{V})^{2\Delta_{W}}}.$ This expression has a nice geometric interpretation in terms of the length of the geodesic connecting the $W$ operators on the two boundaries of an AdS2 background with two parallel shockwaves sourced by the $U$ and $V$ operators. The two parallel shockwaves behave like a single shockwave with a total shift proportional to $4\kappa_{1}\Delta_{U}+4\kappa_{2}\Delta_{V}$ along the $v$ direction. For example, compare the above expression with eq. (28) in [46] or eq. (4.3) of [55]. When $\Delta_{U}=\Delta_{V}=\Delta_{W}=1$ , the result is:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle} \displaystyle=1-4\kappa_{1}-4\kappa_{2}+24\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}+\ldots \displaystyle=1-\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{2\sqrt{3}T_{s}}-\frac{e^{T_{23}}}{2\sqrt{3}T_{s}}+\frac{e^{T_{13}+T_{23}}}{8T_{s}^{2}}+\ldots $$

This can be compared with the perturbative expansion of the six-point function in $1/T_{s}$ . In particular, we will see below that the analytic continuation of the connected six-point function in (4.33) will reproduce the $\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}$ term. But first we will take a small detour and discuss how the scattering result in (5.18) (to all orders in $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ ) can also be derived from the reparametrization path integral.

### 5.2 Double-scaled OTOC from an eikonal resummation

Section 4 showed us that knowing the reparametrization action to cubic order is sufficient to compute the leading (tree-level) contribution to the boundary six-point function. We will now show that, if we focus on the six-point OTOC in the double scaling limit in (5.4), then we can also use the reparametrization path integral in (2.16) to resum all the non-interacting diagrams involving exchanges of the reparametrization mode between the dressed two-point functions of the transverse modes and, moreover, this “eikonal resummation” reproduces the full scattering result in (5.18). The following argument in the case of the six-point OTOC is essentially the same as the analogous argument in the case of the four-point OTOC, which is presented in section 6.3 of [32].

The eikonal resummation is achieved by working with the exact dressed two-point function in (2.20) while truncating the reparametrization action to the quadratic order. The normalized six-point function is then:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle_{\rm eik}}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle} \displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}\epsilon e^{-S_{2}[\epsilon]}\mathcal{B}(x_{1},x_{2})^{\Delta_{U}}\mathcal{B}(x_{3},x_{4})^{\Delta_{V}}\mathcal{B}(x_{5},x_{6})^{\Delta_{W}}. $$

(Here we use the approximation $\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle=x_{12}^{-2\Delta_{U}}+O(T_{s}^{-1})$ , and likewise for $\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle$ and $\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle$ , with the corrections becoming negligible once we take the double scaling limit in (5.4)). We can put the components of the dressed two-point function into an exponential as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}(x_{i},x_{j})^{\Delta} \displaystyle=\left[\frac{(1+\dot{\epsilon}_{i})(1+\dot{\epsilon}_{j})}{(1+\epsilon_{ij}/x_{ij})^{2}}\right]^{\Delta}=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\right)^{\Delta}e^{\alpha_{i}(1+\dot{\epsilon}_{i})+\alpha_{j}(1+\dot{\epsilon}_{j})}\int_{0}^{\infty}dp\frac{p^{2\Delta-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta)}e^{-p(1+\epsilon_{ij}/x_{ij})}. $$

This representation— combined with the identity $\langle e^{f(\epsilon)}\rangle=e^{\frac{1}{2}\langle f(\epsilon)^{2}\rangle}$ if the action is quadratic and $f$ is linear in $\epsilon$ — implies that the six-point function in the eikonal approximation can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle_{\rm eik}}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{2}}\right)^{\Delta_{U}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{3}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{4}}\right)^{\Delta_{V}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{5}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{6}}\right)^{\Delta_{W}}\biggr[e^{\prod_{i=1}^{6}\alpha_{i}}\times \displaystyle\int dpdqd\phi\frac{p^{2\Delta_{U}-1}q^{2\Delta_{V}-1}\phi^{2\Delta_{W}-1}}{\Gamma(2\Delta_{U})\Gamma(2\Delta_{V})\Gamma(2\Delta_{W})}e^{-p-q-\phi+X}\biggr] $$

where

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\big\langle\big(-p\frac{\epsilon_{12}}{x_{12}}-q\frac{\epsilon_{34}}{x_{34}}-\phi\frac{\epsilon_{56}}{x_{56}}+\sum_{i=1}^{6}\alpha_{i}\dot{\epsilon}_{i}\big)^{2}\big\rangle_{0}. $$

The explicit expression for $X$ can be found by performing the Wick contractions with the propagator in (4.4). This gives rise to many different terms, some involving self-contractions (which should be regulated with a short distance cut-off $\delta$ by, e.g., setting $\langle\dot{\epsilon}(0)^{2}\rangle_{0}=\frac{1}{8\pi T_{s}}\log{\delta^{2}}$ ), and the result is invariant under neither the physical nor the gauge $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetries (which is a consequence of us keeping only the quadratic part of the action). However, all these complications wash out once we analytically continue to the OTOC configuration at late times. More precisely, we map the points on the thermal cylinder in (5.2) to the complex plane using $x_{i}=\tan{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}$ and take $T_{1}\sim T_{2}\to\infty$ , $T_{3}\to-\infty$ and $T_{s}\to\infty$ with $e^{T_{12}}/T_{s}$ and $e^{T_{13}}/T_{s}$ held fixed.1212 12 It is important in getting from (5.27) to (5.28) that we send $T_{3}\to-\infty$ at the same time that we send $T_{1}\sim T_{2}\to\infty$ , but the relative rate at which the times are sent to $\pm\infty$ does not matter. In this limit, $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}$ become coincident and $x_{5},x_{6}$ become coincident with $|x_{12}|,|x_{13}|,|x_{14}|,|x_{23}|,|x_{24}|,|x_{34}|\sim e^{-T_{1}}$ and $|x_{56}|\sim e^{T_{3}}$ and the distances between the other pairs of points approaching non-zero values. Consequently, the only contributions to (5.27) that survive in the double scaling limit are:

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle=\frac{p\phi}{x_{12}x_{56}}\langle\epsilon_{12}\epsilon_{56}\rangle_{0}+\frac{q\phi}{x_{34}x_{56}}\langle\epsilon_{34}\epsilon_{56}\rangle_{0}. $$

Performing the contractions using the propagator in (4.4), we have for the first term:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{x_{12}x_{56}}\langle\epsilon_{12}\epsilon_{56}\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{T_{s}x_{12}x_{56}}\bigg[\frac{1}{8\pi}(x_{15}^{2}\log{x_{15}^{2}}+x_{26}^{2}\log{x_{26}^{2}}-x_{16}^{2}\log{x_{16}^{2}}-x_{25}^{2}\log{x_{25}^{2}}) \displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt+b(x_{15}^{2}+x_{26}^{2}-x_{16}^{2}-x_{25}^{2})\bigg] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8\pi T_{s}}\frac{x_{15}x_{26}}{x_{12}x_{56}}\log\left(\frac{x_{15}^{2}x_{26}^{2}}{x_{16}^{2}x_{25}^{2}}\right)+\ldots, $$

where we have put the leading term in a conformally invariant form and $\ldots$ denotes terms that vanish in the double scaling limit. Likewise, the second term in (5.28) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{x_{34}x_{56}}\langle\epsilon_{34}\epsilon_{56}\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8\pi T_{s}}\frac{x_{35}x_{46}}{x_{34}x_{56}}\log\left(\frac{x_{35}^{2}x_{46}^{2}}{x_{36}^{2}x_{45}^{2}}\right)+\ldots. $$

Letting $x_{i}=\tan{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}$ and performing the analytic continuation specified by (5.2)-(5.4), we find:

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle\to-\kappa_{1}p\phi-\kappa_{2}q\phi, $$

where $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ are given in (5.21). Noting that the $\alpha_{i}$ derivatives become trivial and the Schwinger parameters play the role of the light cone momenta, we see that (5.26) precisely reproduces (5.18).

### 5.3 Explicit check of the six-point OTOC

To compare the strong coupling expansion of the scattering result for the six-point OTOC in (5.23) with the analytic continuation of the six-point function, we need the full six-point function in (2.27). This includes a fully disconnected piece, three partially connected pieces, and the fully connected piece. After normalizing by the product of the three two-point functions, the fully disconnected piece gives $1$ , the leading contribution to the partially connected pieces are given by (4.24), and the leading contribution to the fully connected piece is given in (4.33). Then, to perform the analytic continuation, we first map from the line to the circle by replacing $x_{ij}\to\sin{\frac{1}{2}\theta_{ij}}$ and letting the cross ratios be $\xi_{ijkl}=\frac{\sin{\frac{1}{2}\theta_{ik}}\sin{\frac{1}{2}\theta_{jl}}}{\sin{\frac{1}{2}\theta_{il}}\sin{\frac{1}{2}\theta_{jk}}}$ , then fix the $\theta_{i}$ to be as in (5.2)-(5.3), and finally take the limit in (5.4). In particular, we need to determine the behavior of $G(\xi_{ijkl})$ , $G^{\prime}(\xi_{ijkl})$ and $F_{ij;klmn}$ in this limit.

Given the configuration of points specified by (5.2) and (5.3), the three conformally invariant cross ratios are:

$$ \displaystyle\xi_{1234} \displaystyle=1+\frac{3}{-1+2\cosh(T_{12})}, \displaystyle\xi_{1256} \displaystyle=1+\frac{6}{-3+2i\sqrt{3}\sinh{T_{13}}}, \displaystyle\xi_{3456} \displaystyle=1+\frac{6}{-3-2i\sqrt{3}\sinh{T_{23}}} $$

As $T_{13}$ and $T_{23}$ increase from $0$ , $\xi_{1256}$ moves from $-1$ to $1$ clockwise and $\xi_{3456}$ moves from $-1$ to $1$ counterclockwise around the origin, and at late times they are given by

$$ \displaystyle\xi_{1256} \displaystyle\sim 1-2\sqrt{3}ie^{-T_{13}}, \displaystyle\xi_{3456} \displaystyle\sim 1+2\sqrt{3}ie^{-T_{23}}. $$

The leading behavior of the connected four-point functions given by (4.26) in the double scaling limit in (5.4) is:

$$ \displaystyle G(\xi_{1234}) \displaystyle\sim O(1/T_{s}), \displaystyle G(\xi_{1256}) \displaystyle\sim-\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{2\sqrt{3}T_{s}}, \displaystyle G(\xi_{3456}) \displaystyle\sim-\frac{e^{T_{23}}}{2\sqrt{3}T_{s}} $$

Similarly, we find that the leading behavior of the derivatives is:

$$ \displaystyle G^{\prime}(\xi_{1234}) \displaystyle\sim O(1/T_{s}), \displaystyle G^{\prime}(\xi_{1256}) \displaystyle\sim\frac{ie^{2T_{13}}}{12T_{s}}, \displaystyle G^{\prime}(\xi_{3456}) \displaystyle\sim-\frac{ie^{2T_{23}}}{12T_{s}}, $$

And, being careful about smoothly continuing to the correct branches of the various logarithms in (4.32), we find that the leading behaviors of the $F$ functions are given by:

$$ \displaystyle F_{56;1234} \displaystyle\sim O(T_{s}^{0}), \displaystyle F_{34;1256} \displaystyle\sim-\frac{i}{4T_{s}}e^{-T_{12}}, \displaystyle F_{12;3456} \displaystyle\sim\frac{i}{4T_{s}}e^{T_{12}}, $$

Finally, taking $T_{13},T_{23},T_{s}\to\infty$ with $\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{T_{s}}$ and $\frac{e^{T_{23}}}{T_{s}}$ fixed yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle U_{1}W_{5}U_{2}V_{3}W_{6}V_{4}\rangle}{\langle U_{1}U_{2}\rangle\langle V_{3}V_{4}\rangle\langle W_{5}W_{6}\rangle}=1 \displaystyle+\left(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{T_{s}}+\ldots\right)+\left(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{e^{T_{23}}}{T_{s}}+\ldots\right) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{8}\frac{e^{T_{13}+T_{23}}}{T_{s}^{2}}+\ldots $$

The first line gives the leading contributions to the OTOC coming the disconnected diagrams (i.e., the terms in the first line in (2.27)), and the second line gives the contribution from the tree-level connected piece, given in (4.33). We see that (5.37) precisely matches (5.23) in the overlapping terms.

### 5.4 Relationship with the flat-space limit of AdS/CFT

To conclude this section, let us make brief comments on the relation with the flat-space limit of AdS/CFT discussed in the literature, which also expresses the CFT correlation functions in terms of the scattering amplitudes in flat space. The flat space limit of the correlation functions in AdS has been analyzed using various approaches (see e.g.[56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64]). The details of the limit depend on whether the particles are massless or massive, and for massless scatterings, the derivation was explained in detail in section 2.1 of [56] for AdSD≥3, under the assumption that the scattering event happens locally at a single point in the AdS spacetime. In what follows, we explain how their derivation can be generalized to AdSD=2 and how it is related to the formula used in this paper and [47, 32, 53]. We focus on the $2$ -to- $2$ scattering for simplicity but the argument can be readily generalized to higher-point scatterings.

The starting point of their analysis the following rewriting of the bulk-to-boundary propagator $G_{B\partial}$ 1313 13 Here we set $R$ and $\ell_{s}$ in [56] to unity and took $d=1$ .

$$ G_{B\partial}(X,P)\propto\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\beta}{\beta}\beta^{\Delta}e^{-2i\beta P\cdot X}\,, $$

where $X$ and $P$ are the embedding coordinate representations for the bulk and the boundary points respectively (see [56] for details). We next assume that the dominant contribution to the correlation function comes from a small region near the center of AdS (denoted by $X_{\ast}$ ), and approximate the correlation function as1414 14 The formula (5.39) can be viewed as the AdS version of the LSZ formula. In flat space, correlation functions are given by the convolution of amputated Green’s functions with the leg factors, which are the Fourier transforms of the propagators $\sqrt{Z}/(p^{2}+m^{2})$ . Here the leg factors are replaced with their AdS counterparts $G_{B\partial}$ .

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\rangle\sim\int_{R^{1,1}}\prod_{i=1}^{4}dY_{i}G_{B\partial}(X_{\ast}+Y_{i},P_{i})G_{\rm flat}(Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3},Y_{4})\,. $$

Here $Y_{i}$ ’s parametrize a small region near $X_{\ast}$ which can be approximated by $R^{1,1}$ , and $G_{\rm flat}$ is the amputated Green’s function in flat space. We then use the formula (5.38) to get

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\rangle\sim\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{4}d\beta_{j}\beta_{j}^{\Delta_{j}-1}e^{-2i\beta_{j}P_{j}\cdot X_{\ast}}\right)\mathcal{S}\,, $$

with

$$ \mathcal{S}\equiv\int_{R^{1,1}}\prod_{j=1}^{4}dY_{j}e^{-2i\beta_{j}P_{j}\cdot Y_{j}}G_{\rm flat}(Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3},Y_{4})\,. $$

To evaluate $\mathcal{S}$ , we now express the embedding coordinates $X$ and $P$ in terms of the Kruskal coordinates of AdS2 (see [32] for a review),

$$ ds^{2}=-\frac{4dudv}{(1+uv)^{2}}\,, $$

as follows:

$$ X=\left(\frac{1-uv}{1+uv}\,,\frac{u+v}{1+uv}\,,\frac{u-v}{1+uv}\right)\,,\qquad P_{j}=\left(1,\frac{u_{j}+v_{j}}{2},\frac{u_{j}-v_{j}}{2}\right)\,. $$

Here $u_{j}$ and $v_{j}$ parametrizes the boundary of AdS2 and satisfy $u_{j}v_{j}=-1$ , and the center of AdS2 corresponds to $u=v=0$ , namely

$$ X_{\ast}=\left(1,0,0\right)\,. $$

Since $Y_{j}$ ’s describe a small neighborhood of $X_{\ast}$ , they only have two non-vanishing components;

$$ Y_{j}\sim\left(0,\delta u+\delta v,\delta u-\delta v\right)\,. $$

In addition, boundary points at early or late times correspond to either $u_{j}\to\pm\infty$ or $v_{j}\to\pm\infty$ , and the embedding coordinates can be approximated as

$$ P_{j}\sim\frac{1}{2}(0,\bar{p}_{j}^{0},\bar{p}_{j}^{1})\qquad\text{with}\qquad(\bar{p}_{j}^{0},\bar{p}_{j}^{1})=u_{j}\left(1,1\right)\quad\text{or}\quad v_{j}\left(1,-1\right)\,. $$

Thus, dot products $P_{j}\cdot Y_{j}$ ’s, which were originally defined in the embedding space $R^{2,1}$ , can be viewed as inner products in $R^{1,1}$ . Then, $\mathcal{S}$ can be identified with the S-matrix $S_{\rm flat}$ in $R^{1,1}$ and the equation (5.40) can be rewritten as

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\rangle\sim\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{4}d\beta_{j}\beta_{j}^{\Delta_{j}-1}e^{2i\beta_{j}}\right)S_{\rm flat}(p_{j}=-2\beta_{j}\bar{p}_{j})\,. $$

Here we are using a convention in which the momenta $p_{j}$ are all incoming. To make contact with the analysis in [47, 32, 53], we take $p_{2,4}$ ( $p_{1,3}$ ) to be incoming (outgoing) and $p_{1,2}$ ( $p_{3,4}$ ) to be left-moving (right-moving). This corresponds to choosing

$$ \displaystyle p_{1} \displaystyle=2\beta_{1}u_{1}(1,1)=-\frac{2\beta_{1}}{v_{1}}(1,1)\qquad \displaystyle(u_{1}>0,v_{1}<0)\,, \displaystyle p_{2} \displaystyle=-2\beta_{2}u_{2}(1,1)=\frac{2\beta_{2}}{v_{2}}(1,1)\qquad \displaystyle(u_{2}<0,v_{2}>0)\,, \displaystyle p_{3} \displaystyle=2\beta_{3}v_{3}(1,-1)=-\frac{2\beta_{3}}{u_{3}}(1,-1)\qquad \displaystyle(u_{3}<0,v_{3}>0)\,, \displaystyle p_{4} \displaystyle=-2\beta_{4}v_{4}(1,-1)=\frac{2\beta_{4}}{u_{4}}(1,-1)\qquad \displaystyle(u_{4}>0,v_{4}<0)\,. $$

We then change the variable of integration to $p_{j}$ to get1515 15 Here we omitted the prefactor independent of the integration variables, such as $u_{j}^{\Delta_{j}}$ and $v_{j}^{\Delta_{j}}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\rangle\sim \displaystyle v_{1}^{\Delta_{1}}v_{2}^{\Delta_{2}}u_{3}^{\Delta_{3}}u_{4}^{\Delta_{4}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{4}dp_{j}^{0}\left(p_{j}^{0}\right)^{\Delta_{j}-1}\right)e^{-i(p_{1}^{0}v_{1}-p_{2}^{0}v_{2}+p_{3}^{0}u_{3}-p_{4}^{0}u_{4})}S_{\rm flat}(p_{2},p_{4};p_{1},p_{3})\,, $$

This reproduces the formula for the four-point OTOC used in [47, 32, 53] (up to numerical prefactors which we did not keep track of in the discussion above). Essentially the same analysis can be applied to the six-point OTOC and will reproduce the formulas in eq. (5.11)-(5.12) or (5.16).

Let us also point out that the argument here and the argument in [56] both rely on a rather strong assumption that the dominant contribution comes from a small region near $X_{\ast}$ . Although this may seem like a physically reasonable assumption, it would be desirable to prove it or clarify when it can be justified. This is particularly important in view of recent works [61, 63, 64], which showed that similar assumptions do not hold for the scattering of massive particles in certain kinematics. We leave this for future investigation.

## 6 Connected six-point function in static gauge

In this section, we compute the connected six-point function using the Nambu-Goto action in static gauge. This serves as an additional check of the conformal gauge result. The four-point function was computed in static gauge in [14], and we will follow a similar procedure here.

### 6.1 Action and propagators in static gauge

To study the correlation function of identical scalars, we restrict the fluctuations of the string in AdS ${}_{5}\times S^{5}$ to an AdS ${}_{2}\times S^{1}$ subsector. Then the Nambu-Goto action in static gauge reduces to [32]

$$ \displaystyle S[y]=T_{s}\int d^{2}\sigma\sqrt{\det[g_{\alpha\beta}+\partial_{\alpha}y\partial_{\beta}y]}. $$

To find the six-point functions, we can expand the action in powers of $y$ up to sixth order, treating $y$ as a small fluctuation:

$$ \displaystyle S[y]=T_{s}\int d^{2}\sigma\sqrt{g}L_{2n}. $$

We find the vertices

$$ \displaystyle L_{0}=1,\quad L_{2}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}y\partial_{\nu}y,\quad L_{4}=-\frac{1}{8}(g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}y\partial_{\nu}y)^{2},\quad L_{6}=\frac{1}{16}(g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}y\partial_{\nu}y)^{3}. $$

In AdS2, the bulk-boundary propagator has the form [65]

$$ \displaystyle K_{\Delta}(x^{\prime};x,z)=C_{\Delta}\tilde{K}_{\Delta}(x^{\prime};x,z)=C_{\Delta}\left(\frac{z}{z^{2}+(x-x^{\prime})^{2}}\right)^{\Delta}, $$

where $C_{\Delta}=\frac{\Gamma(\Delta)}{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(\Delta+\frac{1}{2})}$ . To deal with the derivatives in vertices, one can use the identity [66]

$$ g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{1}}(x_{1};x,z)\partial_{\nu}\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{2}}(x_{2};x,z)\\
=\Delta_{1}\Delta_{2}[\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{1}}(x_{1};x,z)\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{2}}(x_{2};x,z)-2x_{12}^{2}\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{1}+1}(x_{1};x,z)\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{2}+1}(x_{2};x,z)]. $$

For the exchange diagrams, we also need the bulk-bulk propagator,

$$ \displaystyle G^{\Delta}(a,b)=C_{\Delta}\frac{1}{2u}~{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\Delta,\Delta,2\Delta,-\frac{2}{u}),\quad\quad u=\frac{(z_{a}-z_{b})^{2}+(x_{a}-x_{b})^{2}}{2z_{a}z_{b}}. $$

For $\Delta=1$ , the hypergeometric function reduces to an elementary function,

$$ \displaystyle G^{\Delta=1}(a,b)=C_{\Delta=1}\frac{1}{4}\log{\left(1+\frac{2}{u}\right)}. $$

### 6.2 Computation of correlators

At tree level, the connected six-point function is given by the sum of contact diagrams and exchange diagrams,

$$ \displaystyle\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm conn.}=\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm contact}+\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm exchange}. $$

The contact diagram is shown in Figure 6a. The sum of contact diagrams contributing to the correlation function with six identical massless scalars can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm contact}=-3T_{s}(C_{\Delta=1})^{6}Q_{6y}, $$

Here the factor $(C_{\Delta=1})^{6}$ is from the six boundary-bulk propagators, and $Q_{6y}$ denotes a sum of six-point contact integrals

$$ \displaystyle Q_{6y}=Q_{12,34,56}+\text{14 permutations}, $$

where the first term is given by

$$ \displaystyle Q_{12,34,56}= \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\frac{dzdx}{z^{2}}[g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{1};x,z)\partial_{\beta}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{2};x,z)][g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{3};x,z)\partial_{\nu}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{4};x,z)] \displaystyle\times[g^{\rho\lambda}\partial_{\rho}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{5};x,z)\partial_{\lambda}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{6};x,z)], $$

and other terms are obtained by permuting the external points. (Note that since the derivatives in the vertices of (6.3) combine two external points together, we need to divide the six external points into three pairs, and hence there are 15 combinations, such as $\{12,34,56\}$ , $\{12,35,46\}$ and so on). To understand the overall factor in (6.8), note that for six identical scalars there are $6!=720$ ways to do the Wick contractions. Because there are 15 ways to combine the six points into three pairs, the symmetry factor is $720/15=48$ , and from the vertex in (6.3) we see that the numerical factor in front of each combination should be $-\dfrac{T_{s}}{16}\times 48=-3T_{s}$ .

Using the identity (6.1), the integral (6.10) can be reduced to

$$ \displaystyle Q_{12,34,56}= \displaystyle I_{111111}-8x_{12}^{2}x_{34}^{2}x_{56}^{2}I_{222222}-2x_{12}^{2}I_{221111}-2x_{34}^{2}I_{112211}-2x_{56}^{2}I_{111122} \displaystyle+4x_{12}^{2}x_{34}^{2}I_{222211}+4x_{12}^{2}x_{56}^{2}I_{221122}+4x_{34}^{2}x_{56}^{2}I_{112222} $$

Here, the $I$ -function is defined as

$$ \displaystyle I_{\Delta_{1}...\Delta_{n}}=\int\frac{dzdx}{z^{2}}\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{1}}(x_{1};x,z)\ldots\tilde{K}_{\Delta_{n}}(x_{n};x,z). $$

A method to analytically evaluate the $I$ -functions was given in [31]. For $\Delta_{i}=1$ and even $n$ , the result is

$$ \displaystyle I_{n,\Delta=1}=\frac{\pi}{2(2i)^{n-2}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1,k\neq j}^{n}\frac{(x_{j}-x_{k})^{n-4}}{\prod_{i=1,i\neq j,i\neq k}^{n}(x_{j}-x_{i})(x_{k}-x_{i})}\ln{(x_{j}-x_{k})^{2}}. $$

For $\Delta_{i}>1$ , one may evaluate these integrals using the pinching method discussed in [31].

The exchange diagram is shown in Figure 6b. The corresponding contribution to the connected six-point function can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm exchange}.=T_{s}(C_{\Delta=1})^{6}P_{6y} $$

where $P_{6y}=P_{12,34,56}+{\rm 89~permutations}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle P_{12,34,56}= \displaystyle\int\frac{dz_{a}dx_{a}}{z_{a}^{2}}\int\frac{dz_{b}dx_{b}}{z_{b}^{2}}[g^{\mu\nu}(a)\partial_{\mu}^{(a)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\partial_{\nu}^{(a)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})g^{\rho\lambda}(a)\partial_{\lambda}^{(a)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})] \displaystyle[\partial_{\rho}^{(a)}\partial_{\gamma}^{(b)}G(x_{a},z_{a};x_{b},z_{b})g^{\alpha\beta}(b)\partial_{\alpha}^{(b)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\partial_{\beta}^{(b)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})g^{\gamma\delta}(b)\partial_{\delta}^{(b)}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})]. $$

For exchange diagrams, there are $\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}6!=11520$ ways to do the Wick contraction. One $\binom{4}{1}$ factor corresponds to selecting one bulk point from the four-point interaction vertex, and there are two bulk interaction vertices. $6!$ corresponds to arranging the other six bulk points to the six external points. There are still 15 ways to divide the six points in pairs contracted by derivatives. However, from (6.15) we see that it matters which group we treat as the third group (e.g. which group we put at the position of 56 in (6.15)), and the order of the two points in the third group also matters (e.g. the order of 5 and 6 in (6.15)). Thus, we should have $15\times 3\times 2=90$ independent permutations. For each permutation, there is a symmetry factor $11520/90=128$ . According to (6.3), the numerical factor in front of each permutation should be $128\times\frac{1}{2}\times\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{2}T_{s}=1\cdot T_{s}$ , as written in (6.14).

The integrals (6.15) may be simplified using integration by parts and

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\mu}(\sqrt{g}\partial^{\mu}K_{1})=0, $$

as well as the identity (6.1). This leads to a sum of exchange integrals with no derivatives

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} &P_{12,34,56}=\int\frac{dz_{a}dx_{a}}{z_{a}^{2}}\int\frac{dz_{b}dx_{b}}{z_{b}^{2}}G(x_{a},z_{a};x_{b},z_{b})\times\\
&[2\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})-2x_{15}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})\\
&-2x_{25}^{2}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})-8x_{12}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})\\
&+8x_{12}^{2}x_{15}^{2}\tilde{K}_{3}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})+8x_{12}^{2}x_{25}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{1};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{3}(x_{2};x_{a},z_{a})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{5};x_{a},z_{a})]\\
&\times[2\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})-2x_{36}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})\\
&-2x_{46}^{2}\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})-8x_{34}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{1}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})\\
&+8x_{34}^{2}x_{36}^{2}\tilde{K}_{3}(x_{3};x_{b},_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})+8x_{34}^{2}x_{46}^{2}\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{3};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{3}(x_{4};x_{b},z_{b})\tilde{K}_{2}(x_{6};x_{b},z_{b})].\end{aligned} $$

Putting the contact and exchange diagrams together, the connected six-point function in static gauge is

$$ \displaystyle\langle y(x_{1})...y(x_{6})\rangle_{\rm conn.}=T_{s}(C_{\Delta=1})^{6}(P_{6y}-3Q_{6y}). $$

We were not able to analytically evaluate the exchange integrals (6.17), but we can perform numerical comparisons with the six-point correlator computed in conformal gauge by fixing the values of the six external points and evaluating the various components of $P_{6y}$ and $Q_{6y}$ numerically. We find very good agreement between the analytic result in conformal gauge and the numerical evaluation in static gauge. ## 7 Conclusions

In this work, we studied the six-point function of identical scalars in the half-BPS Wilson line defect CFT in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM at strong coupling. We computed the correlator by studying the dual fundamental string with AdS2 geometry in conformal gauge, in which the interactions between the transverse fluctuations of the string are mediated by a boundary reparametrization mode. The six-point function is sensitive to self-interactions of the reparametrization mode, so the first step in our analysis was to determine the effective action of the reparametrization mode to cubic order. A nice feature of the final result for the six-point function in (4.33) is that it involves only rational functions and logarithms. We also checked the correctness of the conformal gauge approach by setting up the computation in static gauge. In contrast to conformal gauge, we did not manage to compute the six-point functions analytically in static gauge. Instead we evaluated the relevant six-point contact and four-point exchange Witten diagrams numerically for a representative set of external points for the six operators and found agreement with the analytic formula in conformal gauge. This demonstrates the advantage of using the conformal gauge and the reparametrization path integral in evaluating these correlators. Finally, as a further test of our results and to discuss an interesting physical interpretation of the correlator, we also analytically continued the euclidean six-point function to a Lorentzian out-of-time-order configuration which corresponds to a 3-to-3 scattering process on the worldsheet.

One natural extension of the present work would be to study the six-point function of different (protected) scalars on the Wilson line, for instance focusing on the five $\Delta=1$ scalars transforming in the fundamental of $SO(5)$ , which are dual to the fluctuations along $S^{5}$ . The general six-point function is of interest because, unlike the six-point function of identical scalars, it would allow one to test the multi-point superconformal Ward identities conjectured in [26] at the leading order with contributions from fully connected diagrams. Furthermore, one could extract new OPE data from the six-point function that is not readily accessible from the four-point functions at tree level. For example, one could take the coincident limit of three pairs of the six fundamental scalars and extract the OPE coefficient of three copies of the lowest composite scalar transforming in the singlet representation of the $SO(5)$ R-symmetry. Such “three-particle” operators are important also for the four-point function at higher loops since they can appear in the OPE expansion. It is important in this procedure to work with the general six-point function in order to disentangle the operators transforming in different representations of $SO(5)$ . (Recall, for example, that the operators of lowest scaling dimension appearing in the OPE of two fundamental scalars includes both a singlet and a symmetric traceless composite operator.)1616 16 One can also try to extract some OPE data from the six-point function of identical scalars in (4.33), but the data will be averaged over different R-symmetry channels, in addition to involving the usual operator mixing between operators with the same quantum numbers. We were unable to cleanly extract new OPE data from the identical scalar six-point function, even when we supplemented it with input from supersymmetric localization (e.g., the leading rank $-2$ symmetric traceless operator appearing in the OPE of two fundamental scalars is a chiral primary and its OPE data is known exactly [23]).

While we showed in this work that the conformal gauge and the reparametrization path integral simplify drastically the computation of the six-point function of identical scalars — essentially because the transverse action is interacting in static gauge and non-interacting in conformal gauge — the generalization to the six-point function involving all of the five $\Delta=1$ scalars is not straightforward. To compute the general correlator, we would need to study the AdS2 string in an AdS ${}_{2}\times S^{5}$ subspace, which has five transverse modes that, importantly, are interacting even in conformal gauge.1717 17 For example, in stereographic coordinates $y^{m}$ , $m=1,\ldots,5$ on $S^{5}$ , the tranverse action in conformal gauge is $\displaystyle S_{T}[y^{m}]$ $\displaystyle=\frac{T_{s}}{2}\int d^{2}\sigma\frac{\partial_{\alpha}y^{m}\partial^{\alpha}y^{m}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{4}y^{2}\right)^{2}}.$ (7.1) Thus, in addition to the two classes of diagrams we encountered in section 4 involving two reparametrization exchanges and a cubic interaction between reparametrization modes, the computation of the general six point function in conformal gauge will also involve four and six-point contact and exchange diagrams. These are summarized in Figure 8. To make progress in either gauge, it is therefore necessary to find a way of analytically computing the relevant exchange diagrams. (By contrast, for the relevant six-point contact diagrams, one can in principle use the approach described in [31]). The results in this paper can hopefully serve as a stepping stone in that direction.

*Figure 8: In the conformal gauge approach, there are five different classes of reparametrization diagrams that contribute to the connected correlator of six different scalars. The first two classes of diagrams are qualitatively similar to the diagrams in Figure 1 contributing to the six-point function of identical scalars. The remaining three classes of diagrams are new and also involve scalar contact and exchange diagrams.*

Another natural direction one can explore further would be to consider six point OTOC configurations besides the one in (5.4). For example, another double scaling limit that one could take is given by

$$ \displaystyle T_{13}\to\infty,\quad \displaystyle T_{23}\to-\infty \displaystyle T_{s} \displaystyle\to\infty, \displaystyle\frac{e^{T_{13}}}{T_{s}},\frac{e^{-T_{23}}}{T_{s}}:\text{ fixed}. $$

This can be achieved, for instance, by keeping the Lorentzian time of $W$ in (5.1) fixed $(T_{3}=0)$ while sending $U$ to late times ( $T_{1}\to\infty$ ) and $V$ to early times ( $T_{2}\to-\infty$ ). The OTOC in this configuration can be interpreted as a $W$ two-point function, on a background with two crossing or colliding shockwaves, with one left-moving shockwave produced by $V$ and one right-moving shockwave produced by $U$ . This configuration and its shockwave interpretation was studied, in the context of JT gravity and Einstein gravity in AdS3, in [3]. However, making this interpretation of the OTOC precise in the context of the string correlators is slightly subtle. This is because a gravitational shockwave is by definition a spacetime geometry with a discontinuity that arises due to the backreaction to a very high energy wave, but the critical string worldsheet does not have gravity in the usual sense and the notion of “backreaction” is a priori unclear. Instead, as discussed in [55] in the case of a string worldsheet with a single shockwave, one can add “shockwaves” to the string by creating a sharp kink propagating along the string by suddenly changing the acceleration of the boundary of the string. Thus, “shockwaves” on the AdS2 string are related to the “broken” or “segmented” strings studied in [67, 68, 69]. We hope to revisit these geometries, and their relation to higher point OTOCs, in the near future.

## Appendix A Reparametrization mode three-point interaction on the circle

In this section, we rederive the result for the three-point interaction of the reparametrization modes given in (4.14), working with the reparametrization action on the circle rather than on the line. Doing the analysis on the circle allows us to handle the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ zero modes more explicitly.

We will focus only on the contribution of the interacting diagrams on the circle, and will not rederive the full connected six-point function. Recall that we write the boundary mode on the circle as $\tilde{\alpha}(\tau)=\tau+\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , where $\tilde{\epsilon}$ is a small perturbation around the saddle point that we can expand in Fourier modes: $\epsilon(\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}e^{-in\tau}$ . Here, $n=0,\pm 1$ are zero modes of the action that need to be gauge fixed in the reparametrization path integral.

The two ingredients we need to study the three-point reparametrization interaction diagrams are the reparametrization action to cubic order in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ and the dressed two-point function to linear order. After adding a gauge-fixing term $S_{\rm gf}$ , the full action to cubic order is:

$$ \displaystyle S_{L} \displaystyle=S_{\rm gf}+S_{L,2}+S_{L,3}+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{4}), $$

where $S_{L,2}$ and $S_{L,3}$ are given in (3.39) and we pick the gauge-fixing term to be:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm gf} \displaystyle=T_{s}\left[\frac{1}{2a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{0}^{2}+\frac{1}{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{1}\tilde{\epsilon}_{-1}\right]. $$

From the combined quadratic piece $S_{\rm gf}+S_{L,2}$ , we read off the Wick contraction of the Fourier modes:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{m}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=f_{m}\delta_{m+n,0}, \displaystyle f_{m} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}a&m=0\\
b&m=\pm 1\\
\frac{1}{4\pi}\frac{1}{|n|(n^{2}-1)}&\text{otherwise}\end{array}\right. $$

A simple gauge choice is to set $a=b=0$ , which amounts to excluding the $n=0,\pm 1$ modes from $\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , but we can keep $a$ and $b$ general. The $\epsilon$ position space propagator is then:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\epsilon(\tau_{1})\epsilon(\tau_{2})\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{n}e^{-in\tau_{12}}=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[a+2b\cos{\tau_{12}}+\frac{1}{4\pi}\sum_{n\neq 0,\pm 1}\frac{e^{-in\tau_{12}}}{|n|(n^{2}-1)}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[a-\frac{1}{4\pi}+\left(2b+\frac{3}{8\pi}\right)\cos(\tau_{12})+\frac{1}{2\pi}\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}\right)\log\left(4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}\right)\right)\right]. $$

Note that (up to a relabelling of $a$ and $b$ ), this is related to (4.4) by the usual interchange of euclidean distances on the line and chordal distances on the circle.

Meanwhile, the dressed-two point function on the circle $B^{\rm circle}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})$ is given in (2.35), where $\tilde{\beta}$ is the inverse of $\tilde{\alpha}$ , which to linear order in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ is $\tilde{\beta}(\theta)=\theta-\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta)+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{2})$ . The expansion of the normalized dressed two-point function is then:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) \displaystyle\equiv\bigg[2\sin{\frac{\theta_{12}}{2}}\bigg]^{2}B^{\rm circle}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=1+\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{2}), $$

where the linear piece is explicitly

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) \displaystyle=-\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{1}-\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{2}+\cot{\frac{\theta_{12}}{2}}\tilde{\epsilon}_{12}, $$

where we use the shorthand $\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{n}=\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}(\theta_{n})$ and $\tilde{\epsilon}_{ij}=\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{i})-\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{j})$ . Knowing $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ is sufficient to study the contribution of the three-point diagrams to the connected six-point function, which in analogy with (4.10) is given by:

$$ \displaystyle-\langle\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{3},\theta_{4})\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{5},\theta_{6})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,c}, $$

Here “c” stands for “connected” and tells us to contract the $\tilde{\epsilon}$ ’s in the $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ ’s with the three $\tilde{\epsilon}$ ’s in the cubic action. To compute the full connected six-point function, we would also need the quadratic piece $\mathcal{B}_{2}$ .

We will now compute the three-point interacting diagram:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}}=\sum_{a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-ia\theta_{1}-ib\theta_{2}-ic\theta_{3}}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} $$

Given the expression for the cubic action in (3.39) and using the propagator in (A) to Wick contract the different Fourier modes, we have

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)\big[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{m}\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}\tilde{\epsilon}_{p}\rangle_{0}+a\leftrightarrow c+b\leftrightarrow c\big] \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)\big[f_{m}f_{n}f_{p}\delta_{m+a,0}\delta_{n+b,0}\delta_{p+c,0}+a\leftrightarrow c+b\leftrightarrow c\big] $$

(Recall that $p=-m-n$ ). Substituting this into (A.11) and using the three Kronecker deltas to fix $a$ , $b$ and $c$ , we find:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)f_{m}f_{n}f_{p}\left[e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}+\theta_{1}\leftrightarrow\theta_{2}+\theta_{2}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{i}{2}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p(1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1})\left[e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}+\theta_{1}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}+\theta_{2}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}\right]. $$

To get to the second line, we used $f_{p}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}=\frac{p}{4\pi T_{s}}(1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1})$ , which follows from (A). Let’s focus on one term inside the square bracket in (A.13) at a time. There are three different contributions to the sum over $m$ and $n$ , corresponding to the “1,” the “ $-\delta_{p,1}$ ” and the “ $-\delta_{p,-1}$ ” in $1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1}$ . The first is the simplest:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}(m+n)e^{-im\theta_{13}-in\theta_{23}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{3}\biggr[\sum_{m}f_{m}e^{im\theta_{13}}\sum_{n}f_{n}e^{in\theta_{23}}\biggr], \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{3}[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle_{0}]. $$

To get to the second line we used (A.6). In direct analogy with (4.14), we see that the double sum breaks into a product of single sums. This implies that the three-point interaction diagram effectively “factorizes” in terms of products of the $\epsilon$ propagator, as long as the contributions from the “ $-\delta_{p,1}$ ” and the “ $-\delta_{p,-1}$ ” to (A.13) can be neglected. We now show that is indeed the case.

We need to compute:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p\delta_{p,1}e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}=e^{-i\theta_{23}}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{-m-1}e^{im\theta_{12}} \displaystyle\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p\delta_{p,-1}e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}=-e^{i\theta_{23}}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{-m+1}e^{im\theta_{12}} $$

Given that $f_{m}=f_{-m}$ , (A.16) is minus the complex conjugate of (A.15). The last piece that we need to evaluate is then:

$$ \displaystyle k(\theta)\equiv\sum_{m}f_{m}f_{-m-1}e^{im\theta}=\frac{ab}{T_{s}^{2}}\left(1+e^{-i\theta}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{b}{24\pi T_{s}^{2}}(e^{i\theta}+e^{-2i\theta}) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{16\pi^{2}T_{s}^{2}}\sum_{m\neq-2,-1,0,1}\frac{e^{im\theta}}{|m||m+1|m(m^{2}-1)(m+2)}. $$

The remaining sum in (A.17) can be evaluated and simplifies to:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m\neq-2,-1,0,1}\frac{e^{im\theta}}{|m||m+1|m(m^{2}-1)(m+2)}=\frac{e^{-\frac{i\theta}{2}}}{36}\biggr( \displaystyle 3(33-4\pi^{2}+12\pi|\theta|-6\theta^{2})\cos{\frac{\theta}{2}}+20\cos{\frac{3\theta}{2}} \displaystyle+6(|\theta|-\pi)(9\sin{\frac{|\theta|}{2}}+\sin{\frac{3|\theta|}{2}})\biggr). $$

Combining (A.14)-(A.17), eq. (A.13) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\theta_{1}}\left[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\rangle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle\right]+1\leftrightarrow 2+1\leftrightarrow 3+R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}) \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\left(e^{-i\theta_{23}}k(\theta_{12})-e^{i\theta_{23}}k(\theta_{12})^{*}\right)+1\leftrightarrow 2+1\leftrightarrow 3. $$

Eq. (A.19) almost matches eq. (4.14), which we derived working on the line and using analytic regularization to handle the zero modes, except that (A.19) has the extra term $R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ . This term is not zero, but we claim that it does not contribute to (A.10), and therefore can be neglected in the computation of the connected six-point function on the circle. Concretely, the claim is that if we expand each $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ in (A.10) into four $\tilde{\epsilon}$ terms according to (A.9), apply (A.19) to the $64$ different terms, and then sum up all the terms, the contribution from $R$ is zero. This appears tedious to check analytically, but we confirmed it numerically within machine precision for a random sample of values for $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{6}$ .

The rest of the computation of the connected six-point function on the circle proceeds in direct analogy with the computation on the line presented in section 4. The final result— after mapping chordal distances to euclidean distances— matches (4.33).

## Appendix B A conformal bilocal reparametrization action

In this appendix, we give a closed form expression for a bilocal reparametrization action that has the same symmetries as the AdS2 string reparametrization action defined in (2.14). Curiously, the action also precisely matches the string reparametrization action at quadratic and cubic order in the saddle point expansion (but apparently not at higher orders; see footnote 4).

Consider the following bilocal reparametrization action:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal}[\alpha] \displaystyle=-C\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt_{1}dt_{2}\left[\left[\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})-\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}\right]^{h}\frac{1}{|t_{12}|^{2-2h+\eta}}-\frac{1}{|t_{12}|^{2+\eta}}\right]. $$

Here, $\alpha(t)$ is a reparametrization of the line, $h$ and $\eta$ are real parameters, and $C$ is a coupling constant with mass dimension $[C]=\eta$ . This action was studied for the case $2-2h+\eta=0$ in [70, 71], and discussed for the case $\eta=0$ towards the end of appendix G of [33]. We have added a $-1/|t_{12}|^{2+\eta}$ counterterm to make the action finite in the coincident limit $t_{2}\to t_{1}$ as long as $\eta<1$ ;1818 18 The finiteness of (B.1) follows from the fact that in the coincident limit $\displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})-\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}+\frac{1}{6}\{\alpha,t_{1}\}+O(t_{1}-t_{2}),$ $\displaystyle t_{2}\to t_{1},$ (B.2) where $\{\alpha,t\}=-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\ddot{\alpha}^{2}}{\dot{\alpha}^{2}}+\frac{\dddot{\alpha}}{\dot{\alpha}}$ is the Schwarzian derivative. the counterterm is zero in analytic regularization.

We are interested in (B.1) when $\eta\to 0$ . In this special case, the action has two $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetries, just like the string reparametrization action in (2.14), and it is therefore “conformal.” To see this, let $f(t)=\frac{at+b}{ct+d}$ denote a general $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ transformation and let $\alpha_{r}(t)=\alpha(f(t))$ and $\alpha_{\ell}(t)=f(\alpha(t))$ . Given that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{\ell}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}_{\ell}(t_{2})}{(\alpha_{\ell}(t_{1})-\alpha_{\ell}(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}, \displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{r}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}_{r}(t_{2})}{(\alpha_{r}(t_{1})-\alpha_{r}(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\dot{f}(t_{1})\dot{f}(t_{2})\frac{\dot{\alpha}(f(t_{1}))\dot{\alpha}(f(t_{2}))}{(\alpha(f(t_{1}))-\alpha(f(t_{2})))^{2}}, \displaystyle\frac{\dot{f}(t_{1})\dot{f}(t_{2})}{(f(t_{1})-f(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}, $$

one can readily check that $S_{\rm bilocal}$ is invariant under $\alpha\to\alpha_{\ell}$ for any $\eta$ and invariant under $\alpha\to\alpha_{r}$ when $\eta\to 0$ .

Now consider the expansion of the action in (B.1) about the saddle point by letting $\alpha(t)=t+\epsilon(t)$ and expanding in $\epsilon$ . Using (C.1) and integration by parts to simplify the result, we find

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal} \displaystyle=2Ch(1-h)\bigg[\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\frac{\epsilon(t_{1})\epsilon(t_{2})}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}}-2\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\frac{\epsilon(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}t_{12}} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\biggr((1+2h)(3-2h)\frac{\frac{4}{3}\epsilon(t_{1})^{3}\epsilon(t_{2})-\epsilon(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})^{2}}{|t_{12}|^{6+\eta}} \displaystyle\quad+h(1-h)\frac{-2\epsilon(t_{1})\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})+\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})^{2}-\frac{1}{4}t_{12}^{2}\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\dot{\epsilon}(t_{2})^{2}}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}}\biggr)+O(\epsilon^{5})\biggr]. $$

To put this in the Fourier representation, we write $\epsilon(t)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}e^{-i\omega t}\epsilon(\omega)$ and evaluate the $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ integrals using (C.2)-(C.3). This leads to:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal} \displaystyle=\frac{Ch(1-h)}{6}\biggr[\int d\omega\epsilon(\omega)\epsilon(-\omega)|\omega|^{3}-\frac{i}{4\pi}\int d\omega_{1}d\omega_{2}\epsilon(\omega_{1})\epsilon(\omega_{2})\epsilon(-\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})|\omega_{2}|^{4}\text{sgn}(\omega_{2}) \displaystyle-\pi\left(\int\prod_{i=1}^{4}\frac{d\omega_{i}}{2\pi}\epsilon(\omega_{i})\right)2\pi\delta\big(\sum_{i=1}^{4}\omega_{i}\big)\biggr[\frac{(1+2h)(3-2h)}{20}\big(\frac{4|\omega_{4}|^{5}}{3}-|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|^{5}\big) \displaystyle+h(1-h)\bigg(-2|\omega_{4}|^{3}\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|^{3}\omega_{1}\omega_{2}-\frac{3}{2}|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|\omega_{1}\omega_{2}\omega_{3}\omega_{4}\bigg)\biggr]+O(\epsilon^{5})\biggr] $$

As promised, the action in (B.6) precisely matches the string reparametrization action to cubic order given in (3.20) and (3.31), as long as we set $C=\frac{3T_{s}}{\pi h(1-h)}$ .

The analog of (B.1) on the circle (with the counterterm set to zero for simplicity) is:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal}[\alpha] \displaystyle=-C\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\bigg[\frac{\dot{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\dot{\alpha}(\tau_{2})}{\big[2\sin{\frac{\alpha(\tau_{1})-\alpha(\tau_{2})}{2}}\big]^{2}}\bigg]^{h}\frac{1}{\left|2\sin{\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}}\right|^{2-2h+\eta}}. $$

If we set $\alpha(\tau)=\tau+\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , expand in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ , and use (C.4) and integration by parts to simplify terms, we again find that the bilocal action on the circle matches the string reparametrization action given in (3.34) to cubic order.

#### Conformal $k$ -local conformal reparametrization.

Note that (B.1) is constructed by multiplying a reparametrization-dressed conformal two-point function with an undressed two-point function. It is easy to generalize (B.1) and write down a $k$ -local action invariant under two $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetries starting from a pair of conformal $k$ -point functions. In particular, let

$$ \displaystyle G(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})=\langle O_{h_{1}}(t_{1})\ldots O_{h_{k}}(t_{k})\rangle, $$

be any correlator in a 1d CFT of $k$ operators $O_{h_{i}}$ with conformal dimensions $h_{i}$ , and let

$$ \displaystyle\bar{G}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})=\langle\bar{O}_{1-h_{1}}(t_{1})\ldots\bar{O}_{1-h_{k}}(t_{k})\rangle, $$

be any correlator in a 1d CFT of $k$ operators $\bar{O}_{1-h_{i}}$ with conformal dimensions $1-h_{i}$ . Then we define the reparametrization action

$$ \displaystyle S_{k-\text{local}}[\alpha(t)] \displaystyle=C\int\prod_{i=1}^{k}dt_{i}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\dot{\alpha}(t_{i})^{h_{i}}G(\alpha(t_{1}),\ldots,\alpha(t_{n}))\bar{G}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}). $$

This action is also invariant under both $\alpha(t)\to f(\alpha(t))$ and $\alpha(t)\to\alpha(f(t))$ , where $f$ is a general $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ transformation. This follows from (B.3)-(B.5) together with the conformal Ward identity, which says that

$$ \displaystyle G(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\dot{f}(t_{i})^{h_{i}}G(f(t_{1}),\ldots,f(t_{k})), $$

and with an analogous statement for $\bar{G}$ .

Within this construction, (B.11) is unique to the extent that the $k$ -pt function in 1d CFT is unique. For instance, the bilocal action is unique up to normalization $C$ and choice of conformal dimension $h$ , and the $3$ -local action is unique up to normalization and choice of three conformal dimensions $h_{1}$ , $h_{2}$ , $h_{3}$ .

## Appendix C Useful integrals for analytic regularization

In analytic regularization, the following identities hold on the line:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{1}{|t|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{e^{i\omega t}}{|t|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\Delta\right)\Gamma(1-\Delta)|\omega|^{\Delta-1}, \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{e^{i\omega t}}{|t|^{\Delta}t} \displaystyle=-2i\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\Delta\right)\Gamma(-\Delta)\text{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{\Delta}. $$

(The third identity is essentially the derivative of the second identity with respect to $\omega$ ). Likewise, the following identities hold on the circle:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau\frac{1}{|2\sin{\frac{\tau}{2}}|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=2^{1-\Delta}\sqrt{\pi}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{1-\Delta}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\Delta}{2}\right)}, \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau\frac{e^{in\tau}}{|2\sin{\frac{\tau}{2}}|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi(-1)^{n}\Gamma(1-\Delta)}{\Gamma(1-n-\frac{\Delta}{2})\Gamma(1+n-\frac{\Delta}{2})}, \displaystyle\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}. $$

# Chaos and the reparametrization mode on the AdS2 string

## Abstract

We study the holographic correlators corresponding to scattering of fluctuations of an open string worldsheet with AdS2 geometry. In the out-of-time-order configuration, the correlators display a Lyapunov growth that saturates the chaos bound. We show that in a double-scaling limit interpolating between the Lyapunov regime and the late time exponential decay, the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) can be obtained exactly, and it has the same functional form found in the analogous calculation in JT gravity. The result can be understood as coming from high energy scattering near the horizon of a AdS2 black hole, and is essentially controlled by the flat space worldsheet S-matrix. While previous works on the AdS2 string employed mainly a static gauge approach, here we focus on conformal gauge and clarify the role of boundary reparametrizations in the calculation of the correlators. We find that the reparametrization mode is governed by a non-local action which is distinct from the Schwarzian action arising in JT gravity, and in particular leads to $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ invariant boundary correlators. The OTOC in the double-scaling limit, however, has the same functional form as that obtained from the Schwarzian, and it can be computed using the reparametrization action and resumming a subset of diagrams that are expected to dominate in the limit. One application of our results is to the defect CFT defined by the half-BPS Wilson loop in ${\cal N}=4$ SYM. In this context, we show that the exact result for the OTOC in the double-scaling limit is in precise agreement with a recent analytic bootstrap prediction to three-loop order at strong coupling.
